1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. If the generators and the body do not fix the element type, write it, also where a declared type receives the value: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` that no declared type directs gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716).
26	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
27	
28	## Designing a change
29	
30	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
31	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
32	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
33	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
34	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
35	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
36	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
37	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
38	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
39	
40	## Editing
41	
42	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
43

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
42	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
43	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
44	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
45	
46	         git push origin main
47	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
48	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
53

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	Three limits of `ledger.py` (below):
55	
56	- A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no further note.
57	- No command edits a row's claim. `close --claim` takes a corrected one.
58	- Its heading reader does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
59	
60	## Reading the record
61	
62	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
63	
64	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
65	
66	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
67	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
68	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
69	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
70	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
71	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
72	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
73	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
74	
75	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
76	
77	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
78	
79	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
80	
81	## Writing to the record
82	
83	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
84	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
85	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
86	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
87	  - what it means for the work;
88	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
89	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
90	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
91	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
92	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
93	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
94	
95	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
96	
97	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
98	
99	To add a row:
100	
101	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
102	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
103	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
104	
105	To change a row:
106	
107	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
108	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
109	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
117	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
118	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

## 4. The distance stage, per variant

Each run used `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`, niced, from the worktree with the shadow built. I compared each run's `errors.tsv` with `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv` site by site. The comparison masks line and column numbers and generated names, and sorts a union's members. Each run took 180 to 194 s and reported `#crash none` and `#shadow every shadow edit matched the tracked sources`.

| Variant | `#total` | return-type | wellformed | Sites gone against the file | Sites new |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shadow, library unedited | 48 | 2 | 4 | `:130` | — |
| L0 (conditions only) | 44 | 2 | 0 | `:130`; the 4 wellformed of row 433 | — |
| L1 (generic beside `Any`, over `R`) | 46 | 4 | 0 | `:130`; the 4 wellformed | 2 return-type, against the generic: "...should be a subtype of the return type of [\K\](ActualReduction[\T,T\], ActualReduction[\T,K\])->PossibleReductionPair[\T\]" |
| L2 (generic in place, over `R`) | 46 | 2 | 0 | `:130`; the 4 wellformed; the 2 return-type against `Any` | the 2 return-type against the generic; 2 typecheck at `:3225` and `:3229` |
| L3 (generic in place, over `K`) | 44 | 0 | 0 | `:130`; the 4 wellformed; the 2 return-type | 2 typecheck: "Could not check call to function distribute - [\K\]ActualReduction[\R,K\]->PossibleReductionPair[\K\] is not applicable to an argument of type Reduction[\R\]." at `:3225` (`leftDistribute`) and `:3229` (`rightDistribute`) |
| **L4** (L3, and those two over `K`) | **42** | 0 | 0 | `:130`; the 4 wellformed; the 2 return-type | **none** |

L4's table: `#kind typecheck 39`, `#kind export 3`, every other kind 0. Its classes are `X1 3, I3 2, V2 17, G1 1, BR 3, NM 3, GF 1, OT 12`: `R3` (2) and `F1` (4) are gone. Its units are `FlatString 1, FortressLibrary 36, List 5`.

**`FortressLibrary.fss:130`** is `opr BIG LEXICO(g: Generator[\TotalComparison\]) = ...`, which declares no return type. It goes in every run with the shadow, including the run with the library unedited. Row 737 says the checker gives such a function the return type of the api's first declaration of its name in identity-hash order, and the batch 16 record says ":130 still moving through row 737". So it is that order, moved by the shadow's code, and not an effect of `distribute`. Against the shadow's own control, 48, L4 removes exactly the 6 sites of row 433.

So, with the method conditions:
- The team's text as written (L1, L2) clears row 433's 4 wellformed errors and none of its 2 return-type errors.
- Written over `K` (L3), it clears all 6 and costs the 2 forwarders. L4 removes that cost.

+(* A where clause on a method bounds its object's static parameter inside the method: a method of the bound is found on a value of that parameter. *)

+

+end
+object S extends Shows

+end

+end
+

+
+end

object ReversedReduction[\R\](r:Reduction[\R\]) extends Reduction[\R\]
  getter reverse():Reduction[\R\] = r
  getter asString():String = "ReversedReduction(" || r.asString || ")"
  empty():R = r.empty()
  join(x:R,y:R):R = r.join(y,x)
end

(** Invariants:
    join must be associative with identity empty
    unlift(lift(x)) = x
 **)
trait ActualReduction[\R,L\] extends Reduction[\L\]
    lift(r: R): L
    unlift(l:L): R
    (** If this reduction left-distributes over r, return a pair of
        reductions with the same lift and unlift **)
    leftDistribute[\K\](r: ActualReduction[\R,K\]): PossibleReductionPair[\K\] =
        distribute(r)
    (** If this reduction right-distributes over r, return a pair of
        reductions with the same lift and unlift **)
    rightDistribute[\K\](r: ActualReduction[\R,K\]): PossibleReductionPair[\K\] =
        distribute(r)
    (** If this reduction distributes over r, return a pair of
        reductions with the same lift and unlift **)
    (* a hack to avoid the error of overloaded methods *)
    distribute[\K\](r: ActualReduction[\R,K\]): PossibleReductionPair[\K\] =
        NoReductionPair[\K\]
end

trait PossibleReductionPair[\R\] extends Condition[\PossibleReductionPair[\R\]\]
    comprises { NoReductionPair[\R\], SomeReductionPair[\R\] }
end

----
end

trait DistributesOver[\E\] end

(** The identity of + and of juxtaposition for the number type named by the
    static argument alone, with no element in hand: the typecase over a
    %() -> T% witness, the witness of its result type, as %array1% takes
    one of its own.  Each type is tested before its supertypes. **)
additiveIdentity[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 =>
            v: ZZ32 = 0
            cast[\T\](v)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(0))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(0))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(0)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(0))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(0, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(0.0))
        () -> RR64 =>
            v: RR64 = 0.0
            cast[\T\](v)
        else => cast[\T\](0)
    end

multiplicativeIdentity[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 =>
            v: ZZ32 = 1
            cast[\T\](v)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(1))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(1))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(1)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(1))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(1, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(1.0))
        () -> RR64 =>
            v: RR64 = 1.0
            cast[\T\](v)
        else => cast[\T\](1)
    end

object SumProdReductionPair[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\] extends ReductionPair[\T,T\]
    getter outer() = SumReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = ProdReduction[\T\]
end

object MaxSumReductionPair[\T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }\]
        extends ReductionPair[\T,Maybe[\T\]\]
    getter outer() = MaxReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = LiftedCommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\](SumReduction[\T\])
end

object MinSumReductionPair[\T extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], StandardMin[\T\] }\]
        extends ReductionPair[\T,Maybe[\T\]\]
    getter outer() = MinReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = LiftedCommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\](SumReduction[\T\])
end

object SumReduction[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends CommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\]
    getter asString(): String = "SumReduction"
    empty(): T = additiveIdentity[\T\]()
    join(a: T, b: T): T = a + b
    distribute(r: MaxReduction[\T\]): PossibleReductionPair[\Maybe[\T\]\] where { T extends StandardMax[\T\] } =
    MaxSumReductionPair[\T\]
    distribute(r: MinReduction[\T\]): PossibleReductionPair[\Maybe[\T\]\] where { T extends StandardMin[\T\] } =
    MinSumReductionPair[\T\]
end

opr SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): BigReduction[\T,T\] =
    BigReduction[\T,T\](SumReduction[\T\])

opr SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](g: Generator[\T\]): T =
    __bigOperatorSugar[\T,T,T,T\](SUM[\T\](), g)

object ProdReduction[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\] extends CommutativeMonoidReduction[\T\]
    getter asString(): String = "ProdReduction"
    empty(): T = multiplicativeIdentity[\T\]()
    join(a: T, b: T): T = a b
    distribute(r: SumReduction[\T\]): PossibleReductionPair[\T\] =
    SumProdReductionPair[\T\]
end

opr PROD[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\](): BigReduction[\T,T\] =
    BigReduction[\T,T\](ProdReduction[\T\])

# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath
javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" \
      "$D/WorldFlip.java" "$D/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
      > "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" 2>&1
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then
    echo "checker-count: javac failed; see $SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; tail -20 "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 2. run the compiler phase order over the interpreter's library under a private cache
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 10 900 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches="$SCRATCH/caches" \
       -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=$OVERLOAD_CACHE \
       -cp "$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" WorldFlip "$TARGET" ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
RC=$?
if ! grep -q 'has [0-9]* errors\?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ; then
    echo "checker-count: the run printed no error total (rc=$RC); see $SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2
    tail -20 "$SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 3. the table. One row per api the checker named, its own error count as the
#    instrumented checker printed it; then the total, the number of distinct
#    file:line the errors were reported at, and the first crash the checker

    22	/**
    23	 * Represents a list of variable name to static parameter bindings for some
    24	 * context. All instances of this class should be created with `KindEnv.makeFresh`
    25	 * or with the `extend` method.
    26	 */
    27	abstract sealed class KindEnv extends StaticEnv[StaticParam] {
    28	
    29	  /** My type. */
    30	  type Env = KindEnv
    31	
    32	  /** My binding type. */
    33	  type EnvBinding = KindBinding
    34	
    35	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given node. */
    36	  def extend(node: Node): KindEnv =
    37	    new NestedKindEnv(this, KindEnv.extractNodeBindings(node))
    38	
    39	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given nodes. */
    40	  def extend[T <: Node](nodes: Iterable[T]): KindEnv =
    41	    new NestedKindEnv(this, nodes.flatMap(KindEnv.extractNodeBindings))
    42	
    43	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given node. */
    44	  def extend(node: Node, where: Option[WhereClause]): KindEnv = {

runRanges(x: Indexed[\Boolean,ZZ32\]): List[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\] =
  (BIG BOXPLUS[i <- 0 # |x|] (if x[i] then RangeSet(0, <|[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\] i:i |>, 0) else SingleRange(1))).ranges

opr BIG BOXPLUS[\T\](): BigReduction[\RunRanges, RunRanges\] =
   embiggen[\RunRanges\](fn(a,b) => a BOXPLUS b, SingleRange(0))

trait RunRanges comprises { SingleRange, RangeSet }
  getter ranges(): List[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\]
  opr BOXPLUS(self, x: RunRanges): RunRanges
end

object SingleRange(n: ZZ32) extends RunRanges
  getter ranges() = <|[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\] |>
  opr BOXPLUS(self, other: SingleRange) = SingleRange(n + other.n)
  opr BOXPLUS(self, other: RangeSet) = RangeSet(n + other.left, other.ranges, other.right)
end

object RangeSet(left: ZZ32, ranges: List[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\], right: ZZ32) extends RunRanges
  opr BOXPLUS(self, other: SingleRange) = RangeSet(left, ranges, right + other.n)
  opr BOXPLUS(self, other: RangeSet) =
    if right + other.left >= 2 then
      RangeSet(left, ranges || other.ranges, other.right)
    else
      (ps, p) = ranges.extractRight.get
      (q, qs) = other.ranges.extractLeft.get
      RangeSet(left, ps || <| p.lower:q.upper |> || qs, other.right)
    end
end

lift(r:R): R = r
    unlift(r:R): R = r
  end

  object MIMapReduceReduction[\R extends Any\](j:(R,R)->R, z:R) extends MonoidReduction[\R\]
    getter asString():String="MIMapReduceReduction from embiggen"
    getter id(): R = z
    join(a:R, b:R): R = (j)(a,b)
  end

  embiggen[\T\](j:(T,T)->T, z:T) : Comprehension[\T,T,T,T\] =
      Comprehension[\T,T,T,T\](fn (x) => x, MIMapReduceReduction[\T\](j,z), fn (x) => x)

  trait AssociativeReduction[\R extends Any\] extends ActualReduction[\R,Maybe[\R\]\]
    getter id(): Nothing[\R\] = Nothing[\R\]
    join(a: Maybe[\R\], b: Maybe[\R\]): Maybe[\R\] =
        if av <- a then
            if bv <- b then
                Just(simpleJoin(av,bv))
            else
                a

## 4. Settled already

- **`embiggen`'s site (row 631, 1 site): not an ask.** P-27 sets the way: the library's own typed shape, `MapReduceReduction[\R\](j, z: R)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3691`), which `MIMapReduceReduction` and `embiggen` would follow (`:3700`, `:3714`). The review queue sorts it as routine (item 124). Its cost is on record: the declared types of its callers in `Library/Map.fss:197`, `Library/IntMap.fss`, `Library/PrefixMap.fss`, `Library/Pairs.fss:75` and the team test `ProjectFortress/tests/WordCountSmall.fss:76` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md:160`). So it is the coordinator's call for the next library rung, listed for his review. It comes back as an ask only if that rung finds that a walk value moves, or if the coordinator reads his word on the team's demos as covering the team test.
- **The list half's other way, a bound on the list's element.** P-42 rules it out: the library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, and a bound on `LexicographicOrder`'s element would make a list of tuples, functions or `()` impossible to write (`explorations/reviews/tuple-comparisons-judgement.md`, way 1c). So the list half waits on the `where` clauses (P4).
- **The bare `Nothing` (row 331; F-21).** P-90: not tried before `where` clauses work. A point for the coordinator, not an ask: the specification's own "Not allowed" `Empty` shows that a singleton extending `List[\T\]` for every `T` is refused by instantiation exclusion with or without a `where` clause (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:469-513`), and F-167's sentence bars its form. So building `where` clauses will not reopen it, and P-90's wording, which ties it to them, may want a line.
- **Arithmetic in a size, the first array fork.** P-55, answered.
- **The element width, the model's sized types, and the store that puts `double[]` under the generic traits, the last three array forks.** P-85: open with no default, and returning after the switch-over. The model's sized types are also P-87's: a diff shown to him before anything is built, in phase 5. When they return, the order is the width, then the model's types, then the store, since every type line of the model's diff and every store follows from the width (`explorations/reviews/array-design-ways.md`, section 8). Owed before then: their plain explainers (review-queue item 37), and an answer to his question why `RR64` and not `RR32`; the one reason on record is the Python reference's float64 values (P-85).

39:\section{Type Parameters}
83:\section{Nat and Int Parameters}
130:\section{Bool Parameters}
151:\section{Dimension and Unit Parameters}
185:\section{Operator Parameters}
313:\section{Where Clauses}
316:\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}
466:at the start of this section.}
&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
\end{Grammar}


Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
in a \KWD{where} clause.
A \KWD{where} clause begins with
\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
and separated by commas.


A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
static variables that are not also static parameters.
The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.


A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
\begin{itemize}
\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
\item an arithmetic constraint,
\item a boolean constraint,
\item a unit equality constraint,
\item a \KWD{coerces} constraint (described in
  \secref{coercion-declarations}), or
\item a \KWD{widens} constraint (described in
  \secref{coercion-declarations}).
\end{itemize}
A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
\KWD{where} clauses.

A \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static argument
in an \KWD{extends} clause.
Such an occurrence would make the declared trait or object a subtype of
one instantiation for each type that the variable may stand for,
which instantiation exclusion forbids
(\secref{trait-types} and \secref{trait-decls});
the second of the three declarations below shows why.
\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
allowed, each with the way to write it.}

In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
it is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
Static parameters are invariant:
\EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
only if \VAR{S} and \VAR{T} are the same type.
A value of one instantiation is widened to another by a function
whose bounded static parameters state that one argument extends the other:
%trait C[\S\]
%  getter item(): S
%end
%object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
%widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\:\VAR{item}()\COLON S\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}S\rrbracket(\VAR{item}\COLON S) \KWD{extends}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\VAR{widen}\llbracket{}T, S \KWD{extends}\:T\rrbracket(c\COLON C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket)\COLON C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(c.\VAR{item})\)
\end{Fortress}
so that, where a trait \TYP{Dog} extends a trait \TYP{Animal} and \VAR{d}
is a \EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Dog}\rrbracket},
\EXP{\VAR{widen}\llbracket\TYP{Animal}, \TYP{Dog}\rrbracket(d)} is a
\EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Animal}\rrbracket} with the same item.
The library's covariant collections are written this way.
\revision{revival-covariance}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves,
and gave the declaration above as the way to express covariance.

component XXXEmptyGroupSumRungF
export Executable

(*) explorations/compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md

object M7(v: ZZ32) extends AdditiveGroup[\M7\]
    getter zero(): M7 = M7(0)
    opr +(self, o: M7): M7 = M7((v + o.v) MOD 7)
    opr -(self): M7 = M7((7 - v) MOD 7)
end

run() = do
    println("REACHED")
    e = SUM[\M7\][i <- 0#0] M7(i)
    assert(e.v, 0, "reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\"; evaluation/reduction.tex, subsection \"Reduction Variables\"; algebraic-constraints.tex, section \"Operators and Their Properties\"")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
(* The library's overload families that the compiled checker refused, called under walk, and BIG MIN and BIG MAX over total comparisons (row 461). *)
component LibraryOverloadFamilies
import List.{...}
export Executable

opr :(x: String, y: String): String = x "-" y

inOrder(g: Generator[\ZZ32\]): String = do
    s: String := ""
    for x <- seq(g) do s := s || x end
    s
end

run() = do
    a = array[\ZZ32\](3).tabulate(fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => if i = 1 then 5 else i + 1 end)
    assert(inOrder(a), "153", "an array's elements in order are 1, 5, 3")
    assert(inOrder(a MIN 2), "122", "an array MIN a scalar takes the smaller of each element and the scalar")
    assert(inOrder(2 MIN a), "122", "a scalar MIN an array takes the smaller of the scalar and each element")
    assert(inOrder(a MAX 2), "253", "an array MAX a scalar takes the larger of each element and the scalar")
    assert(inOrder(2 MAX a), "253", "a scalar MAX an array takes the larger of the scalar and each element")
    v = array[\RR64\](2).tabulate(fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 2.0 i - 1.0)

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

#!/bin/bash

set -u
MODE=$1; DIR=$2; shift 2

BASE=/home/user/fortress-base17
OLDC=$NEWT/tmp/old-caches
NEWC=$NEWT/tmp/rung-library-distribute/skeptic/new-caches
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_THREADS=${FORTRESS_THREADS:-1} TMPDIR=$NEWT/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$NEWT/tmp"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
[ -d $NEWC ] || cp -a $NEWT/default_repository/caches $NEWC
cd $DIR && mkdir -p out
for P in "$@"; do
  case $MODE in
    walk) A=("$P.fss") ;;
    typecheck) A=(typecheck "$P.fss") ;;
    compile) A=(compile "$P.fss") ;;
  esac
  $BASE/explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh $BASE $OLDC "${A[@]}" > out/$P.old.txt 2>&1; echo "exit=$?" >> out/$P.old.txt
  FORTRESS_HOME=$NEWT FORTRESS_CACHES=$NEWC $NEWT/bin/fortress "${A[@]}" > out/$P.new.txt 2>&1; echo "exit=$?" >> out/$P.new.txt
  sed -i -e "s#$NEWT#TREE#g; s#$BASE#TREE#g" out/$P.old.txt out/$P.new.txt
  if diff -q out/$P.old.txt out/$P.new.txt >/dev/null; then echo "== $P SAME"; else echo "== $P DIFFERS"; fi
done
EOF

(* IntMap's combine calls its function on each key both maps hold, and its two map functions on the parts that only one map holds. *)
component IntMapCombine
import IntMap.{...}
export Executable

addValues(k: ZZ64, a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32): Maybe[\ZZ32\] = Just[\ZZ32\](a + b)
dropKey(k: ZZ64, a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32): Maybe[\ZZ32\] = Nothing[\ZZ32\]
keepAll(m: IntMap[\ZZ32\]): IntMap[\ZZ32\] = m
dropAll(m: IntMap[\ZZ32\]): IntMap[\ZZ32\] = {[\ZZ32\] }
tenTimes(m: IntMap[\ZZ32\]): IntMap[\ZZ32\] = m.map[\ZZ32\](fn (k: ZZ64, v: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 10 v)

run(): () = do
    noEntry = {[\ZZ32\] }
    oneEntry = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 10}
    sameKey = {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 5}
    otherKey = {[\ZZ32\] widen(2) |-> 5}
    farKey = {[\ZZ32\] widen(-100) |-> 7}
    eight = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k | k <- 0#8}
    upper = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> 100 | k <- 4#8}

    assert(noEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, noEntry).isEmpty, true, "two empty maps combine to the empty map")
    assert(noEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, oneEntry).check(), oneEntry, "the empty map combined with a map gives that map's part through the second map function")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, noEntry).check(), oneEntry, "a map combined with the empty map gives its part through the first map function")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, sameKey).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 15}, "two one-entry maps on one key combine their values by the function")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](dropKey, keepAll, keepAll, sameKey).isEmpty, true, "a key whose function answers Nothing is left out")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, otherKey).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 10, widen(2) |-> 5}, "two one-entry maps on different keys combine to both entries")
    assert(otherKey.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, oneEntry).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(1) |-> 10, widen(2) |-> 5}, "the order of the maps does not change the entries of two maps on different keys")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, dropAll, dropAll, otherKey).isEmpty, true, "two one-entry maps on different keys share no key")

    both = {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then k elif k < 8 then k + 100 else 100 end) | k <- 0#12}
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, upper).check(), both, "two many-entry maps combine the keys both hold and keep the others")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, dropAll, dropAll, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> k + 100 | k <- 4#4}, "two many-entry maps with both map functions dropping keep only the keys both hold")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](dropKey, keepAll, keepAll, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then k else 100 end) | k <- 0#12, k < 4 OR k >= 8}, "two many-entry maps with the function answering Nothing keep the keys only one holds")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, tenTimes, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then k elif k < 8 then k + 100 else 1000 end) | k <- 0#12}, "the second map function maps the keys only the second map holds")
    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, tenTimes, keepAll, upper).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k < 4 then 10 k elif k < 8 then k + 100 else 100 end) | k <- 0#12}, "the first map function maps the keys only the first map holds")

    assert(eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, oneEntry).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k = 1 then 11 else k end) | k <- 0#8}, "a many-entry map combined with a one-entry map on a key it holds")
    assert(oneEntry.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, eight).check(), {[\ZZ32\] widen(k) |-> (if k = 1 then 11 else k end) | k <- 0#8}, "a one-entry map combined with a many-entry map on a key it holds")
    assert(|eight.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, farKey).check()|, 9, "a many-entry map combined with a one-entry map on a key below all of its keys")
    assert(farKey.combine[\ZZ32,ZZ32\](addValues, keepAll, keepAll, eight).check().member(widen(-100)).get, 7, "a one-entry map on a key below all of a many-entry map's keys keeps its entry")

usage: ledger.py [-h] COMMAND ...

The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the

                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                appends TEXT to row N's notes
  close N --commit HASH --test NAME [--note TEXT] [--claim C] [--class C]
        [--spec C] [--found-by C]
                             after the fix has landed: HASH must be in HEAD's
                             history and NAME a test under the test folders;
                             writes the one-line FIXED row (the claim's first
                             sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed
                             HASH; full text: history, row N`); the options
                             give cells the old row lacks in the template's form
